 ASEAN Digital Economy Advances, But Oil and Haze Hurdles Remain
 Jayanty Nada Shofa 
 November 20, 2026 | 8:30 am 
 SHARE 
 URL berhasil di salin.
 President Prabowo Subianto and other Southeast Asian leaders as well as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi do the ASEAN handshake at the ASEAN-India Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. (Antara Photo/Bayu Pratama S) 
 Jakarta. The recent ASEAN Summit in Manila saw the group’s digital economy agenda leap forward, but the bloc still needs to get rid of the transboundary haze for good and put its regional oil stockpiling plan in motion.
 The Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) has become one of, if not the most, concrete outcomes of the Philippines’ chairship. This pact will harmonize rules related to digital payments, online commerce, and data flows. Negotiations began when Indonesia was the bloc’s chair in 2023. 
 President Prabowo Subianto touted the DEFA as a “great opportunity to ensure future growth with the potential to unlock a $2 trillion digital economy by 2030”, double the business-as-usual scenario of $1 trillion. He was upbeat that it can bring “tangible benefits” to businesses, workers, and youth.
 As the document awaits the lawmaking process, IT expert Heru Sutadi told the Jakarta Globe that the DEFA could enable Indonesian digital products to tap other ASEAN markets. The subsequent interoperability of payment systems can slash costs for small enterprises. The DEFA can also turn into an investment magnet. 
 ADVERTISEMENT
 Heru, however, cautioned that the pact’s benefits risk being limited to countries with better infrastructure, human capital development, and regulatory support, especially if ASEAN doesn’t come up with “infrastructure funding and digital capacity building”  for the members that need to catch up.
 “The benefits with DEFA are not automatic for Indonesia. We must make sure our businesses can compete and not turn into a market for foreign digital platforms,” Heru said.
 Haze Go Away 
But the DEFA can’t be a smoke screen for the persistent haze. Indonesian forest fires have spewed toxic smoke to Singapore and Malaysia, even leading to diplomatic friction. The Manila talks saw Prabowo apologizing to the neighbors amid an easing haze from rainfall and fire-fighting efforts.
 ASEAN is seeking to activate its Jakarta-based haze coordinating center, but at least six members must ratify a regional agreement before the facility can operate. Vietnam is the first to have ratified the document. ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn said that two unnamed countries had already followed suit. Asked about the timeline of the center’s full operations, Kao only answered that “it was important to get [the ratification] fast as haze knows no borders”.
 Brawijaya University international relations lecturer Aswin Ariyanto Azis doubts a “new body” — in this case the haze center — could be the silver bullet. He added: “We are not short of hotspot data or cooperation agreements. What we are lacking is the political courage to take action against the businesses behind the wildfires.”
 Indonesia and Singapore have agreed to form a task force meant to follow the money trails of companies linked to the haze. Calvin Khloe of the foreign policy think tank FPCI said that ASEAN should ponder on Singapore’s proposal of expanding this task force into a regionwide platform for better information-sharing. 
 “But the problem is the [bilateral] task force has not really taken shape. But Singapore wants it to be expanded so I suppose they need to work it out,” Calvin said.
 Aswin struck a pessimistic tone on the expansion, saying that things would not change much if its job is only to exchange information and hold meetings.
 “The political courage to solve the problem usually disappears when the smoke clears. Let’s see if Singapore is brave enough to interfere with businesses when it chairs ASEAN next year,” Aswin said.
 Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong receives the ceremonial handover gavel from Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the ASEAN Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. (Antara Photo/Bayu Pratama S) 
 Oil Disruptions 
ASEAN has been mulling sharing its fuel during supply disruptions, especially after the Strait of Hormuz blockade, as over half of its crude comes from imports. Despite the days-long Manila gathering, Kao said that the scheme remained at an “early stage,” albeit with ongoing discussions. The Philippines claimed that Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, and Manila had “agreed to” the stockpiling — either to be the host country or put their inventories in their neighbors. The United Arab Emirates reportedly intends to chip in.
 Muhammad Ishak Razak of CORE Indonesia said the mechanism was indeed “feasible” by starting small using existing facilities and only involving a few countries. An “oil ticketing arrangement” where an entity pays the other to access its storage facility is also a likely option.
 “But it wouldn’t be easy. [ASEAN] has not agreed on the rules on the supply release, payment, and access rights. The existing APSA petroleum agreement is still voluntary and commercial,” Ishak said.
 He warned of the proposal’s possible impact on national energy security if the scheme doesn’t have clear rules on who gets the oil first and the price mechanism.
 “Indonesia’s storage capacity stands at only 25-26 days. Indonesia doesn’t have a dedicated buffer reserve. Regional commitments must not deplete domestic supplies,” Ishak said, while reminding that Jakarta is a net crude importer.
 The Jakarta-based think tank ERIA and business lobby IBC agreed to become “knowledge partners” for pilot projects on oil stockpiling.  The Philippine energy firm PNOC-EC inked deals with Indonesia's Interport Mandiri Utama and The Shell Company of Thailand Limited. They are set to adopt an oil ticketing scheme.
